engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Thinking Process
chess.body: Every move: 1. What did my opponent just do? (threats?) 2. What are my candidate moves? (at least 2-3) 3. Calculate each candidate 2-3 moves deep. 4. Use LPDO check. 5. Make the move. Don't play on impulse. Even 30 seconds of structured thinking eliminates 80% of blunders. This process is the difference between 800 and 1200 Elo.

book.author: Michael Gerber
book.chapter: Work ON Your Business, Not IN It
book.lesson: Gerber's central argument: most small businesses are started by technicians who love their craft — a baker who opens a bakery, an accountant who opens a firm. They are brilliant at the technical work but have no idea how to build a business. The fatal mistake: working in the business (doing the craft) instead of on it (building the systems). The goal is to build a business that can run without you. Every process should be documented. Every role should have a system. The business should be a franchise prototype — replicable, teachable, and not dependent on any one person's genius.
book.key_quote: If your business can't run without you, you don't own a business — you own a job.
book.action: Identify one thing only you do in your work that, if systematised, could be done by someone else. Write the system this week.
crux: The fatal assumption: understanding the technical work means understanding a business that does that work.
Every owner is three people — Technician (does), Manager (orders), Entrepreneur (envisions) — usually 70/20/10.
Working in your business is not working on your business.
Business life cycle: Infancy (you do everything), Adolescence (past capacity), Maturity (systems run it).
Most businesses collapse in adolescence, when the owner's capacity is the ceiling.
Build the business as the prototype for 5,000 more, even if you only ever want one.
The Franchise Prototype: systems-dependent, not people-dependent.
Work on the business as if you intend to sell it. That forces documentation.
Hire ordinary people and give them extraordinary systems, rather than hunting for extraordinary people.
Your Primary Aim comes before the business plan. What is the life this business is for?
Seven development programmes, starting with the innovation–quantification–orchestration cycle.
Quantify everything. Without numbers you cannot see the business at all.
Documentation is what turns a job into an asset.
learnings: Being excellent at the craft is what traps most skilled people in a job they own.
If it only works when you do it, you built a job, not a business.
Systems are the product. The output is a by-product.
Quantify before you optimise, or you are guessing.
examples: Sarah's pie shop: superb baker, failing business. She loved baking and hated owning, and never noticed the difference.
McDonald's succeeded on operational systems, not recipes — every store reproducible by teenagers.
The hotel Gerber describes ran on documented detail: turndown at a set time, a specific glass, a specific note. The system produced the feeling.
adapt: Document the newspaper pipeline so it survives you not touching it. GitHub Actions is already most of the way there.
Codex must run without your hands in it — that is the difference between a product and freelancing.
Quantify the content engine: posts per week, score distribution, follower delta. No numbers, no view.
Every manual step in the trading stack is a step that fails when you are busy interviewing in Dubai.

interview_tech.q: How would you decide between renting and buying a distribution centre?
interview_tech.a: Compare NPV of both over the same horizon at the same discount rate. Rent is an operating commitment — now on balance sheet under IFRS 16 anyway — with flexibility to exit. Buying ties up capital and carries residual value risk, but fixes occupancy cost and creates an asset. The real question is strategic, not arithmetic: how confident are you in the network design over 15 years. If the answer is 'not very', pay the premium for optionality.

interview_tech.q: Your group operates in a country that introduces 15% VAT. What breaks?
interview_tech.a: Systems and margin, in that order. Systems: tax codes on every SKU, correct treatment of zero-rated versus exempt lines, input recovery on mixed-use costs, and the reverse charge on imported services — all of which must be in the ERP before go-live, not after. Margin: if you absorb VAT rather than pass it through, gross margin falls by roughly the VAT rate on the absorbed portion. Cash: output VAT is collected before it is remitted, so there is a temporary working capital benefit that people mistake for profit.

interview_soft.q: How do you stay current technically while managing?
interview_soft.a: Be specific and verifiable. Name the standard you last read in full and why, the technical update you attended, the thing you built yourself recently rather than delegated. Vague answers about 'reading widely' land badly with technical interviewers. The strongest version connects it to a decision: 'I went back through IFRS 16 properly when we hit the lease modification question on the Indonesian stores, and that changed how we structured the renewal.'

interview_soft.q: Where do you think retail is heading in the next five years?
interview_soft.a: Have a view and defend it with numbers, not trends. Something like: physical stores stop being judged on their own sales as fulfilment and returns blur the channels, which breaks conventional store P&L and forces a catchment-level view; margin pressure shifts from price to cost-to-serve; and in the Gulf specifically, corporate tax and e-invoicing professionalise finance functions that were previously light. Then say what you would do about it in the role you are interviewing for.

cfo_field.q: The controller who never leaves the close never becomes CFO.
cfo_field.a: The job you are promoted out of is 'the person who produces the numbers'. The job you are promoted into is 'the person who decides what to do about them'. If your calendar is 70% close, reconciliation and audit prep, you are demonstrating that you are excellent at the job you already have. Push the close down: a well-run retail group closes in 5 working days, and every day you shave buys back roughly 12 days a year of capacity to spend on decisions instead of production.

cfo_field.q: The Gulf pays for scarcity, not for years.
cfo_field.a: Salary in the region tracks the intersection of skills, not the length of the CV. CA plus genuine FP&A plus retail plus a system implementation is a much rarer combination than any one of them is deep. If you are negotiating, the leverage is in naming the intersection, not in listing the years. And check the structure: basic versus allowances changes gratuity, which is calculated on basic salary alone.

lichess_games.analysis: Increase your pawn‑storm speed: after 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5, play 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.Bd3 cxd4 6.Qxd4 f6 earlier—cut average move time from 33 s to under 20 s to avoid 2‑move mistakes.
lichess_games.standout: A genuine comeback: the engine had you 3.4 pawns down at the low point and you still won.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early central pawn tension: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6, develop the knight to f6 before ...Be7, and exchange on d4 promptly to avoid cramped positions; this will reduce unnecessary piece shuffling and improve your average centipawn loss by ~15 ELO points.
Focus on converting the queen’s side majority into a concrete passed pawn before move 30; you wasted ~15 seconds on indecisive maneuvers.
lichess_games.standout: Decided on the clock, not the board — the position was still playable when time ran out.

lichess_summary.session_summary: **Verdict:** You dominate every opponent you face, but you’re winning on autopilot—your 100 % record is built on a single, predictable opening that any prepared adversary can dismantle. Stop relying on that comfort zone; study at least two contrasting systems (e.g., a solid …e6 setup and a sharp …c5 counter‑gambit) and force yourself to play them in every training game. Your next step is to schedule a 30‑minute post‑mortem after each win, deliberately looking for moments you felt “safe” rather than “forced,” and turn those into deliberate practice drills.

lichess_puzzle.tip: King activity and pawn structure dominate. Technique over tactics here.
